The ennanga is an African bow harp used by the Ganda people of Uganda; it is a plucked instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 322.11. The soundbox is made from a single piece of wood, roughly hemispherical, with an antelope skin stretched over it as a resonating membrane and held at the bottom by leather thongs. The neck rises from inside the body through a small hole in the membrane and curves upward, and seven or eight strings run from a wooden piece inside the body, through the skin, to tuning pegs on the neck, which sometimes carry metal rattles to refine the timbre. The player plucks the strings, and it is usually used to accompany male singing, and within a strictly structured tradition makes each performance different.
恩南加弓豎琴為烏干達干達人的弓豎琴，屬非洲弓豎琴傳統。此類樂器與古埃及無前柱豎琴: The ennanga is the bow harp of the Ganda people of Uganda, part of the African bow-harp tradition. Instruments of this kind are close to the pre-pillar harps of ancient Egypt, and early wall paintings go back to 3000 BCE; by 2500 BCE there were already mature images of bow harps. Klaus Wachsmann held that the portable bow harp travelled from Egypt down the Nile to East Africa, with Uganda at its centre, and in the mid twentieth century 12 of 25 ethnic groups had a harp tradition. When the angular harp rose in later ancient Egypt, the bow harp survived in folk and peripheral regions. The ennanga is of the spoon-in-cup type, with the neck resting loosely on a bowl-shaped soundbox and held by string tension.
